detail.abstract:
Public-company governance increasingly depends on a legal inference: that disclosure before purchase amounts to consent to the terms disclosed. SpaceX's initial public offering exposes the limits of that inference. The company offered public investors economic exposure to one of the most valuable and strategically significant firms in the world while pairing that exposure with an unusually restrictive governance structure, aided by recent changes to Texas corporate law. The market's acceptance appears to vindicate the disclosure-based premise of federal securities law: investors were warned about what they were buying and bought anyway. 

But disclosure is not consent, and consent is not negotiation. SpaceX reveals the emergence of a public-market contract in which governance terms are standardized, nonnegotiable, enforcement-displacing, and increasingly distributed through market infrastructure rather than individualized investor choice. When retail investors purchase they do not bargain over arbitration provisions, dual-class stock, derivative-suit thresholds, forum rules, board independence, or index eligibility. Retirement savers may acquire exposure through index funds, pension portfolios, and employer-sponsored plans without choosing the issuer's governance terms, often without knowing when the stock was bought. Yet, they are bound by the terms of the bargain. 

This phenomenon is corporate Lochnerism. Like Lochner-era freedom of contract, it treats formal assent as sufficient while minimizing consideration of the structural conditions that shape the bargain. In public markets, those conditions include issuer power, exchange competition, index inclusion, and passive-investment infrastructure. Corporate and securities law increasingly treat these standardized governance restrictions as voluntary bargains even when many affected investors neither negotiate nor directly choose them. What both bodies of law lack is a vocabulary for governance adhesion. SpaceX shows that the central question is no longer whether investors may knowingly make a bad bargain, but when law should stop treating the bargain as meaningfully theirs to make.

detail.abstract: Firms hand machines more tasks and more decisions every quarter, yet the research on human-machine collaboration measures automation, trust, and oversight and rarely measures the culture that surrounds them. This paper reviews that research and the early evidence from practice. It then offers a framework that adapts the author's 2010 work on Collaboration Quadrants to the age of AI. The framework sorts work by task (defined or open-ended) and by decision (human decides or machine decides), which yields four quadrants: Assistant, Advisor, Operator, and Agent. Each quadrant needs its own culture. The paper treats the machine as a new member of a working team, projects how the quadrants shift over the next twelve months, and closes with seven tests for moving work toward the machine and four habits that build the culture. A machine may hold the decision. A human always holds the mandate.

detail.abstract: Safety is among the most regulated and most measured dimensions of organizational life, yet marketing scholarship has engaged it mainly through product-harm crises and recalls, leaving everyday safety to operations, human resources, and compliance. This conceptual paper argues that, for business-to-business (B2B) suppliers, safety is a market-based asset: a capability that customers experience as part of the offering, that shapes satisfaction and relationship outcomes, and that investors price when it is material and credibly communicated. Integrating research on occupational safety, organizational buying, relationship marketing, the satisfaction-profit chain, market-based assets, strategic capabilities, and voluntary disclosure, we develop the Safety-as-Market-Asset (SMA) framework. The framework links managerial framing to safety capability, safety performance, B2B customer satisfaction, customer outcomes, and firm value, and it specifies three conditions that govern the size of these effects: strategic integration, safety communication (materiality and conduct-communication alignment), and service discourse quality. We advance eleven propositions. The most novel is a dual-audience tension: disclosure and greenwashing research imply that investors discount talk that is not backed by conduct, whereas signaling theory implies that B2B buyers can reward only the safety they can observe. The paper repositions safety from a cost center to a value driver in marketing strategy and marketingfinance research, and it closes with managerial guidance and a research agenda.

detail.abstract: Firms make promises to many audiences at once: product and service promises to customers, values promises to employees, strategic and sustainability promises to investors. Marketing has long studied one of these gaps, the gap between what a firm promises customers and what it delivers, but has treated the others as the province of management, accounting, and finance. This conceptual paper argues that the alignment between what a firm says and what it does is a single strategic phenomenon that spans audiences, and that managing it is a marketing capability. Integrating research on expectation disconfirmation and service gaps, preannouncements and vaporware, organizational decoupling and behavioral integrity, psychological contracts, cheap talk and voluntary disclosure, and greenwashing, we develop the Promise-Delivery Alignment (PDA) framework. The framework defines the promise-delivery gap by its direction (overpromising versus underpromising), domain, and audience; introduces a typology of four alignment positions; and specifies the audience-specific mechanisms through which gaps affect customer satisfaction, employee commitment, and firm value. We advance eleven propositions. Among them, we propose that overpromising harms more than underpromising helps once delivery is observable, that underpromising carries a hidden cost at the point of acquisition, that promises on dimensions irrelevant to an audience erode credibility even when kept, and that gaps revealed to one audience spill over to others. We close with implications for managers, investors, and regulators and an agenda for measuring the say-do gap at scale.

detail.abstract: Motivated by platform governance policies, regulatory scrutiny, and longrun marketplace management, we study ranking and assortment decisions under visibility and market-outcome constraints. Consumers follow a cascade choice model, inspecting products sequentially and purchasing the first satisfactory product. We distinguish between flexible-ranking settings, where the platform jointly optimizes assortments and rankings, and fixed-ranking settings, where it only chooses assortments. We characterize the structure and tractability of optimal display policies under several constraints. For endogenous rankings, assortment optimization becomes unnecessary, and the platform's decision reduces to optimizing the ranking. We derive tractable solutions under minimum market-share constraints. For top-𝑘 visibility constraints, we develop a simple constant-factor approximation for the associated separation problem and a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme for the original randomizedranking problem that satisfies all display constraints exactly. For exogenous rankings, minimum display probability constraints induce randomized assortment policies with a nested structure: there exists an optimal policy that randomizes over at most linearly many assortments, each containing the unconstrained revenue-maximizing assortment as a subset. This structure yields a polynomial-time algorithm. Minimum market-share constraints are also tractable through a duality-based approach. We find that market share requirements can reshape display policies and substantially increase the value of ranking flexibility. We also study the estimation problem when the offered assortment is unobservable. This paper provides guidance on how visibility, governance, and regulatory requirements affect ranking management.

detail.abstract: Business-to-business (B2B) marketing theory assumes that the buyer is a person, or a committee of people, who perceives risk, forms relationships, responds to persuasion, and feels satisfied or dissatisfied. AI agents that search, compare, negotiate, and recommend on behalf of buying organizations break that assumption. This conceptual paper asks what happens to B2B marketing when the entity that first reads a supplier's proposal, parses its disclosures, and scores its performance is a machine. Integrating research on organizational buying, artificial intelligence in marketing, algorithmic decision making, search and switching costs, customer satisfaction, signaling, voluntary disclosure, and agency theory, we develop the Machine-Mediated Exchange (MME) framework. The framework models B2B exchange as a triad of a principal (the buying organization), an AI purchasing agent, and a supplier, and identifies the information an agent weighs: supplier talk, supplier proof, and third-party evidence. We advance eleven propositions. Agents are expected to raise the weight of verifiable, machine-legible attributes; to apply attributes that human buyers value but neglect, such as supplier safety, more consistently; to discount emphasis that is not backed by evidence; to make silence about real capability costly; and to erode relationship-based retention unless satisfaction is continuously demonstrated. Agents also optimize the proxies they are given, inviting metric gaming, content manipulation, and convergence on the same suppliers. We outline implications for suppliers, buyers, and regulators and a research agenda for a discipline whose customer is increasingly a machine.

detail.abstract: Patient safety culture (PSC) and patient-centred care (PCC) are essential for resilient health systems, yet both remain underexplored in Myanmar. This study investigates organisational, behavioural, and cultural barriers to PSC and PCC by examining the perspectives of healthcare workers and the general public. A cross-sectional survey was conducted using the Hospital Survey on Patient Safety Culture (HSOPSC) framework and Best–Worst Scaling (BWS) to capture preference shares (%) across key attributes. Responses from both healthcare workforce and patients were analysed using Microsoft Excel, SPSS, and OriginPro, with visualisations generated through Flourish Studio.The findings reveal notable divergences and overlaps between groups. The general public prioritised respectful communication (68% best score), timely emergency attention (72%), and dignity in care (61%). Healthcare workers, by contrast, emphasised teamwork (65%), supervisor support (59%), and clear handover practices (62%). Both groups identified staff shortages (65% workforce reporting frequent shortages), hierarchical barriers, and fear of blame (reported by 38% of staff as inhibiting error reporting) as critical threats to patient safety. Preference share analysis confirmed alignment on communication clarity but revealed gaps in perceptions of institutional accountability.Bridging patient and workforce perspectives is vital to achieving safer, more patient-centred healthcare in Myanmar. Policy actions should focus on strengthening structured communication and handover practices, addressing workforce shortages and burnout, fostering a non-punitive safety culture, and embedding PCC principles into national health policy. These findings provide an empirical foundation for reforms aligned with the WHO Global Patient Safety Action Plan 2021–2030 and the Sustainable Development Goals.

detail.abstract: The growing integration of artificial intelligence into software delivery increases AI-tool usage, operational signals, and feedback speed, but technological adoption alone does not establish organizational adaptation. Previous research on the Data-Empirical Agility Model (DEAM) conceptualized adaptation latency as the temporal gap between an operational signal and coordinated organizational response but did not provide a reproducible event-level measurement protocol. The object of the study is organizational adaptation in AI-augmented multi-team software delivery. The study aims to develop a context-specific protocol for measuring the interval from a qualifying trigger to durable organizational reconfiguration and to specify the conditions required for its subsequent empirical evaluation. The methodology combines construct and prior-art analysis, event-level operationalization, retrospective calibration using a longitudinal five-Scrum-team case, and prospective validation design. The protocol represents an adaptation episode through T0–T4: qualifying trigger, recognition of the need for response, response commitment, implementation onset, and durable organizational reconfiguration. T4 is assigned only when five conditions are jointly satisfied: observable change, operational enactment, persistence, traceable provenance, and independence from subsequent performance outcomes. On this basis, the study operationalizes L04=T4−T0 as a candidate temporal measure rather than a validated new construct. Subsequent evaluation requires inter-rater reliability, robustness of the T4 persistence criterion, discriminant validity, temporal validity, and incremental validity. Retrospective application of the protocol to one organizational adaptation episode within the five-team case demonstrates the practical separation of the initial trigger, local piloting, commitment to a scaled response, implementation onset, and durable change in organizational practice. For this episode, the interval from the approximately dated T0 to T4 was about 184 days, while the T1 boundary had lower temporal precision because of the retrospective nature of the evidence. The example illustrates application of the protocol but does not constitute empirical validation of L04 or establish its causal effect on software delivery outcomes. The practical value of the proposed approach lies in providing a structure for prospective data collection that separates AI exposure, organizational response, durable reconfiguration, and subsequent outcomes. Future empirical evaluation may support, refine, or reject the proposed operationalization.

detail.abstract: The United States reported more COVID-19 deaths than any other nation. Yet in 2019 the Global Health Security Index had ranked it the best-prepared country on earth. It spent 16.6% of its GDP on health care, far more than its peers, and the Affordable Care Act's main coverage programs had been in place since 2014. This paper asks a blunt question. Was the American death toll driven by denial or by a lack of resources? It answers through an exploratory comparative policy analysis of the United States, Finland, Sweden, and the Netherlands. The analysis uses reported deaths, all-cause excess mortality, preparedness scores, health spending, insurance coverage, paid sick leave rules, and a harmonized measure of public trust. Under World Health Organization estimates, the United States recorded about 2,730 excess deaths per million people in 2020 and 2021, compared with 1,631 in the Netherlands, 1,073 in Sweden, and 513 in Finland. It had the highest rate of the four under all six published estimation methods reviewed. The evidence does not support a simple shortage of resources. It is more consistent with three deficits: a trust deficit, a coverage deficit, and a coherence deficit, each of which political denial appears to have deepened. The paper proposes these as the Denial-Deficit Framework, a hypothesis for future testing rather than a causal finding. Using a social determinants of health (SDOH) lens, it shows why health insurance, one SDOH factor among many, could not protect people who lacked paid sick leave, room to isolate, or a trusted public health voice. It closes with policy implications and measurable indicators.

detail.abstract: Agentic AI is extending artificial intelligence from prediction and content generation toward systems capable of autonomous goal pursuit, planning, tool use, memory, adaptation, coordination, and action. This shift creates an adoption problem that differs from conventional technology acceptance because stakeholders must decide not only whether to use an AI system, but also whether, when, and to what extent decision and action authority should be delegated to it. This comprehensive survey synthesizes the technological, agentic, human, organizational, responsible-AI, governance, and institutional factors shaping Agentic AI adoption across emerging application contexts. The analysis identifies perceived usefulness, reliability, autonomy, competence, controllability, explainability, trust, perceived risk, organizational readiness, human oversight, accountability, security, and regulatory conditions as central determinants. It further distinguishes adoption intention from delegation willingness, actual use, and sustained use, organising distinct stages of increasingly autonomous use without assuming that delegation is a newly identified outcome. Building on this synthesis, the survey proposes the Agentic AI Adoption and Delegation Framework (AIA-DF), which links system and agentic characteristics, organizational readiness, and governance assurance with trust, perceived control, perceived risk, adoption intention, delegation willingness, and sustained use. The survey also identifies unresolved challenges involving construct definition, measurement, trust calibration, trajectory explainability, oversight thresholds, governance assurance, cross-domain validation, and high-stakes adoption. The resulting framework provides a foundation for empirical research and responsible organizational deployment of increasingly autonomous AI systems.

detail.abstract: With growing interest in energy efficiency, reduced carbon footprints, fair trade, and other prosocial aspects of consumer goods, governments have increasingly relied on consumer tax credits to promote the purchase of qualifying products. This, in turn, places added emphasis on firms to deliver products that align with this evolving demand. However, achieving alignment is complicated by complex global supply chains and associated coordination frictions. This paper examines the consequences of consumer tax subsidies in a model where firms in an uncoordinated (decentralized) supply chain undertake actions to develop and sell prosocial products. We find that contrary to volume-related inefficiencies, supply chain participants effectively coordinate on prosocial actions. Despite conflicting self-interest and a reluctance to bear costs for others, there is unanimity among participants on prosocial actions, and the agreed actions match those of a coordinated (centralized) supply chain. Such coordination arises despite consumers being the recipients of tax benefits while firms incur the costs. In this context, we demonstrate that welfaremaximizing tax subsidies incentivize aggressive firm commitments to prosocial actions so as to also boost production levels. Finally, we show that firms overstating their practices ("greenwashing") and coordinated prosocial actions can co-exist, though such overstatement can come at a cost.

detail.abstract: Digital technologies are increasingly presented as tools for expanding entrepreneurial opportunities among young people, yet evidence from low-income and fragile contexts remains limited. This short communication examines how access to and use of digital platforms relates to entrepreneurial development among university students in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, with particular attention to agribusiness. Using survey data from 199 university students in Lubumbashi, we examined the use of Facebook, YouTube, websites, specialized applications, WhatsApp and artificial intelligence (AI), and their associations with business-idea development, project implementation and improvement, and service-improvement skills. Binary logistic regression showed differentiated relationships across platforms. AI use was positively associated with business-idea development (OR = 2.244, p = 0.021), while application use was strongly associated with project implementation and improvement (OR = 3.199, p = 0.001). YouTube was positively associated with service-improvement skills (OR = 2.111, p = 0.049). These findings suggest that digital inclusion policies in the DRC should move beyond connectivity toward purposeful digital entrepreneurship and agribusiness training. Universities, agricultural extension services and entrepreneurship-support institutions can use digital platforms as complementary infrastructure for youth enterprise development.

detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence (AI) governance frameworks have largely developed around predictive models operating at discrete decision points, emphasizing model validation, fairness auditing, documentation, and point-in-time impact assessment. As AI systems become embedded in institutional workflows and begin to structure how decisions are sequenced, cases prioritized, and resources allocated over time, these model-centric approaches become structurally incomplete. This paper argues that the central governance challenge for such systems lies in maintaining the lifecycle integrity of delegated execution: the continuity of institutional control across delegated AI execution. In formal terms, lifecycle integrity refers to the sustained institutional alignment of operational objectives, delegated execution, monitoring mechanisms, accountability structures, and intervention capacity throughout runtime conditions. 

The paper first reconstructs the implicit assumptions of model-centric governance and shows why they fail once AI is embedded in workflows and execution is delegated. It then develops lifecycle integrity as a runtime-governance construct with five dimensions: delegation horizon, runtime visibility, accountability continuity, objective integrity, and supervisory continuity. Finally, it applies the framework to 15 documented deployments across welfare and financial administration, criminal justice and policing, and healthcare, drawing on court judgments, regulatory investigations, parliamentary inquiries, audit reports, and peer-reviewed evaluations. 

Across cases such as automated welfare-enforcement pipelines, risk-based sentencing tools, live facial-recognition deployments, and proprietary clinical-prediction models, the analysis identifies recurring patterns of governance decoupling: extended delegation horizons without effective control points, opaque or misaligned runtime visibility, fragmented accountability across vendors and institutions, drift or failure in objective integrity, and reactive rather than continuous supervision. The paper concludes that institutions are undergoing a governance transition from governing models to governing delegated execution, and that lifecycle integrity is a structural precondition for navigating this transition. It outlines design implications for building runtime-governance architectures that can preserve institutional control continuity as organizations adopt increasingly workflow-integrated and agentic AI systems.

detail.abstract: Organizations using generative artificial intelligence for population analytics need to know whether aggregate agreement preserves the conditional differences their decisions require. We evaluate recorded antidepressant prescribing across 528 demographic-condition groups covering 720,009 reported visits in OCHIN community health data (Bensken et al., 2025). We distinguish pooled agreement, ordering six nonexclusive drug classes within groups, and differentiating groups within classes. Among 16 open-weight and seven commercial language models, the strongest common-prompt pooled correlations are 0.780 and 0.858, compared with 0.796 for a descriptive frequency reference and 0.921 for a group-held-out random forest. Strong within-group ordering coexists with uneven within-class differentiation, especially weak for selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors. Several other model-class combinations retain meaningful conditional signals. Exploratory rule-generation results and a preliminary single-seed local-example experiment show heterogeneous responses to additional information. We develop an information-target fit interpretation without treating output performance as a direct measure of model knowledge. Aggregate correspondence does not establish conditional population validity, and recorded-care fidelity remains distinct from treatment appropriateness, equity, and patient benefit.

detail.abstract:
Pay-or-Okay models, also known as cookie paywalls or ‘consent or pay’, ask users either to accept
tracking for behavioural advertising or to pay for access without it. This paper synthesises nine
empirical studies on these models and compares how European regulators assess them under the GDPR.
Publisher data show that about 99% of users choose the tracking option when faced with such a wall.
In a survey experiment, around nine in ten participants consented when only ‘pay’ and ‘consent’ were
offered; when a free option with non-personalised advertising was added, the odds of choosing tracking
fell by about 97%. Paying usually reduces tracking but does not always remove it, and the model now
appears on business, technology, entertainment and health websites as well as news sites. Regulatory
responses diverge. The EDPB’s Opinion 08/2024 is limited to large online platforms, national
authorities apply different tests, and Amendment 1427 to the Commission’s Digital Omnibus proposal
would allow controllers to answer a refusal of consent with a paid alternative. We recommend audits of
paid options and clearer banner information, at least one free alternative without behavioural
advertising, restrictions on Pay-or-Okay for websites processing sensitive data, and treating designs that
impose materially more tracking than standard consent banners as a breach of fairness. The findings are
relevant to the EDPB’s forthcoming guidelines on ‘consent or pay’ models.

detail.abstract: Professional services firms moved AI-assisted delivery from pilot to production between 2024 and 2026. This paper takes up five questions that follow. What does a firm sell once clients can license the same models? Who answers for an error that passes through five agents? Does a validator role build judgment, or only train the next model? What separates a governed AI deliverable from one that fails its own citations? And what can a new hire expect three years out? The paper treats commercial model, operating design, and behavioral incentives as one design problem. Its main mechanisms are an Emergency Override Protocol that makes declaring a suspension cheaper than hiding one; a paired metric that pays partners for keeping human capability only when delivery efficiency also holds; a rotating Challenger role grounded in vigilance research; an experience-portfolio talent model built around two to three years of tenure and an alumni network; and a two-tier operating model for data-residency regimes, with Saudi Arabia as the worked case. The paper argues that the firm's lasting advantages are its independence from the client's frame, accountability that a regulator can reach, and a data feedback loop competitors cannot buy.

detail.abstract: Cloud computing has become an important part of education, professional work, communication, file management, and digital collaboration. Microsoft cloud services such as Microsoft 365, OneDrive, Teams, Outlook, SharePoint, and Copilot allow users to perform many activities through internet-based platforms. At the same time, continued cloud use requires users to place considerable reliance on the provider's cybersecurity capabilities. This study develops a Protection Motivation Theory (PMT) and Trust Theory model to examine how perceived severity, perceived vulnerability, response efficacy, self-efficacy, and response cost relate to cybersecurity trust and continued use intention toward Microsoft cloud services in Bangladesh. The proposed research uses a quantitative, cross-sectional survey design with a five-point Likert questionnaire and PLS-SEM-oriented analysis. To demonstrate the complete analytical workflow, a empirical dataset containing 400 observations was generated. The empirical analysis produced acceptable internal consistency across all constructs, with Cronbach's alpha values ranging from 0.797 to 0.862. The structural demonstration indicated that perceived severity, perceived vulnerability, response efficacy, and self-efficacy were positively associated with cybersecurity trust, whereas response cost showed a negative association. Cybersecurity trust was positively associated with continued use intention. These results are illustrative only and are not evidence from real respondents. The study provides a complete methodological and analytical framework that can be reused after genuine survey data are collected.

detail.abstract: Operations leaders rarely end the day as they planned it. A morning agenda is routinely interrupted by urgent on site incidents and by requests from other departments such as finance, suman resources, procurement and supply chain. This paper, written as a practitioner reflection, describes the operations leader's day as three competing demands: the planned agenda, immediate on site issues, and cross-departmental coordination. Drawing on more than 17 years of operations experience in five countries, it proposes a simple time allocation heuristic, protect about half of the working day for the planned agenda, hold flexible capacity for incidents, and set aside at least one hour daily for crossdepartmental communication. The framework is connected to established research on managerial work, fragmented work and attention switching. The paper is experience-based and does not report empirical data; the proposed allocations are practical rules of thumb offered for testing in future research.

detail.abstract: Sponsored advertising platforms let a seller set a bid on every keyword, and a large catalogue produces tens of thousands of them. This paper presents PRISM, a weekly bid control framework that stratifies keywords by intent, by product attributes such as colour, size and fabric type, and by program, and controls each stratum against the stock that stands behind it. Intent is mapped from the attributes a shopper names in a query. The framework reads four performance windows, a priority quartile, a rolling memory and a revenue weighted availability signal, and returns a new bid for every keyword. Availability is built from the stock keeping unit to the attribute cell to the program. A cost of sales limit flags program and colour cells for review, every cell is optimised by the thresholds of the rule sheet, and a brand posture, aggressive or defensive, bounds the size of any move. The paper separates the science of the engine from the art of the judgement layer that sets its envelope, and shows how automation and AI agents can operate inside that envelope. Nine propositions with proofs state what the engine can and cannot do to a bid, and a reference implementation passes randomised property tests. The method does not depend on the product category, and the paper maps it to five other sectors. It specifies the method, the controls and an evaluation protocol, and it reports no measured outcomes.

title: Report-Driven ETL Synthesis: Deriving Data Pipelines from an Analyst Query Workload and a Target Report Specification

detail.abstract: Analytics engineering routinely bridges two mismatched artefacts. Analyst SQL queries encoding operational business logic, and target report specifications defining required grains and service levels. The ETL pipeline connecting them is still designed by hand. We formalise this intermediate step as a derivation problem, using the query workload and report specification as complementary bounds to synthesise dimensional schemas, execution DAGs, and self validating regression suites. We present Report-Driven ETL Synthesis (RDES), an eight-stage framework: query normalisation, column-level lineage extraction, semantic consolidation with explicit conflict reporting, grain and measure-class inference, dimensional model derivation from functional dependencies, physical operator planning including change-data-capture and materialisation selection, orchestration synthesis, and, finally, automatic derivation of a validation harness in which the original queries serve as oracles for the pipeline that replaced them. A worked retail example shows the three places where the derivation is forced to stop and ask a human: semantic conflicts between queries, measures whose aggregation is holistic, and report attributes with no lineage into any source. We have implemented stages Normalise through Model, with verification, and ran them on TPC-H, TPC-DS and a seeded retail case. All 121 benchmark queries parse and yield lineage, in 0.19 s and 1.99 s respectively, scaling linearly. Against the published TPC-DS schema as a third-party gold standard the derivation recovers all 7 fact tables and all 17 dimensions exactly. Conflict detection reaches recall 0.91–0.94 and flags none of 77 benign syntactic variants. The derivation does not vary between runs, where a frontier model's TPC-H fact recall ranged from 0.667 to 1.000 across three identical prompts. Stages Provision and Schedule are specified but neither implemented nor evaluated, and no pipeline was ever executed on an ETL platform.

detail.abstract:
Most debate about AI in customer support asks whether machines should replace people. This paper asks a different question: where should the AI sit? It argues that in urgent technical support, where a customer's business is stopped and money is being lost, the most efficient design puts a trained person in front of the customer and the AI behind that person. During the call, the AI does three things, and only three: it prompts the agent with what to ask or check, it forecasts the likely cause and the time to fix, and it lays out ranked options. Around those three, it prepares a summary of the customer's devices before the agent says hello and drafts the case notes afterwards. The agent accepts, edits, rejects or flags every output, and only the agent speaks to the customer. The paper names this the Pilot-in-Command Doctrine, after the aviation rule that the pilot, not the automation, is the final authority over the aircraft.

The paper makes six contributions. First, it sets out the Human Ahead, AI Behind design and contrasts it with AI in front (bots) and with no AI. Second, it maps each AI function to the phase of a support call where it saves time, and argues that the largest gain may come from shortening the long tail of slow diagnoses rather than the typical call. Third, it proposes a stricter efficiency measure, time to a solved problem, analyzed as a time-to-event outcome, which counts an outcome only when the customer confirms it and the case is not reopened within 7 days. Fourth, it describes how a four-month onboarding program, The Answer Academy, trains agents to stay ahead of the AI rather than defer to it. Fifth, it sets out the economics of skill development: what the training costs, what faster learning and longer tenure are worth, and who should pay. Sixth, it sets out a staged internal field test, run by the venture that operates the pilot and registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF) before it begins, whose stages end on pre-set conditions rather than calendar dates, and whose de-identified data and code will be released openly through OSF. It states in advance which results would weaken the thesis. Along the way, the paper shows how the design makes the 2-2-2-15 service standard achievable (2 clicks, 2-step verification, 2 minutes to a person, a 15-minute outcome) and how it lets one agent support any brand, device or operating system.

detail.abstract: Why can substantial spending on data technology create little enterprise value, while a coordinated organizational transformation creates value across many business units? This paper models a data-driven organization through six distinct capabilities: People, Data Quality, Data Architecture, Data Governance, Automation, and AI. People, Quality, and AI jointly determine outcome reliability; Automation changes execution volume; Architecture changes integration costs and technical reach; Governance determines authorized reach. These mechanisms yield a joint reliability boundary: scaling creates operating value above the boundary and scales expected losses below it. Consequently, some complementarities change sign, and AI cannot compensate for sufficiently weak data or judgment. The same model connects lower resource requirements per successful outcome to investment costs and derives a discounted condition for improving reliability before scaling. A six-state accumulation law links central investment to reusable contributions from local applications. Under profitable-only local adoption, a low-capability region is invariant without sponsorship, while central coordination or cost sharing can unlock shared investment. Synthetic examples illustrate configuration dependence and sustained capability renewal. The framework is an explicit theoretical hypothesis about organizational structure, with testable predictions about error exposure, cross-domain reach, and investment sequencing.

title: Barrage Linguistic Features and Consumer Engagement Dynamics: Evidence from Online Product Review Videos
affiliations: University of Macau, University of Macau, University of Macau, affiliation not provided to SSRN and National Sun Yat-sen University

detail.title: Barrage Linguistic Features and Consumer Engagement Dynamics: Evidence from Online Product Review Videos

affiliations.org_name: Unaffiliated Authors - affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.abstract: Barrages are brief on-screen messages posted by online consumers while a product review video is playing. In this paper, we investigate how linguistic features of barrages co-vary with the volume and emotional arousal of consumer engagement with product review videos. Specifically, we focus on two dimensions of linguistic features: arousal language (affective dimension) and descriptive specificity (cognitive dimension). Based on large-scale barrage and weekly consumer engagement data, we adopted the Panel Vector Autoregression model to estimate the dynamic relationships between consumer engagement and barrage linguistic features. Our results show that the arousal language and descriptive specificity of the previous barrages will be positively associated with the volume of barrages in the following week. However, the arousal language and descriptive specificity of the prior week's barrages will be negatively associated with the emotional arousal of barrages in the following week. We further tested the heterogeneity of video information richness and influencers’ arousal in videos. This research advances the theoretical and practical understanding of consumer-generated content in electronic commerce by showing how barrage linguistic cues shape consumer engagement with product review videos. The findings offer useful implications for digital platforms, influencers, and marketers seeking to improve engagement management.

title: The Dual Value Theory of Content: Reconstructing the Value System of Content in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
affiliations: Wuhan University of Technology and Wuhan University of Technology

detail.title: The Dual Value Theory of Content: Reconstructing the Value System of Content in the Age of Artificial Intelligence

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract: In the age of artificial intelligence, content has acquired a value property that exceeds its conventional communicative function, and became machine-learning corpus. This article builds the Dual Value Theory of Content (DVT), meaning content now simultaneously carries a cultural attribute, realized by human readers via dissemination, knowledge transmission, and civilizational accumulation, and a data attribute, realized by machine learning via training, alignment, evaluation, and retrieval. The two attributes are situated against three historical revaluations, where the scarce object moves from the means of reproduction to human attention and then to trustworthy machine-learnable knowledge. Four propositions including value co-embodiment, quality homology, scarcity reversal, and value circulation state the relations between the two values, while a five-dimensional framework operationalizes the theory. Article contributes at: audience as a variable rather than a constant; non-additivity with distributive consequences; a resource-based account of scarcity reversal; and an operational instrument. The design is theory construction; propositions carry falsification conditions.

title: All is (Not) Fair in EU AI Law

detail.abstract: Fairness is a common reference point in debates on artificial intelligence (AI), yet its meaning as a legal term remains unclear. This paper examines what the term ‘fairness’ and its derivatives do in four EU instruments governing AI: the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the Digital Markets Act (DMA), the Digital Services Act (DSA) and the Artificial Intelligence Act (AI Act). Each instrument is read against a four-stage model of the AI lifecycle (design, development, deployment and redress), taking account of legislative history and enforcement practice to 2026. Fairness under the GDPR governs the processing of personal data rather than the treatment of persons by an AI system, and its content remains contested. Fairness under the DMA primarily denotes the policy objective of ‘fair markets’, and its use as an operative term is largely devoid of substantive meaning. The DSA pursues much of what fairness is invoked to achieve through transparency, diligence and the balancing of fundamental rights, and its enacting terms never apply the term to an algorithmic process. The AI Act refers to fairness in its recitals but imposes no fairness requirement on operators or AI systems, and the European Parliament’s proposed fairness principle was dropped from the adopted text. The paper argues that EU lawmakers have shown a distaste for explicit fairness requirements in instruments regulating AI, and that any operative content fairness acquires under the AI Act is likely to come from harmonised standards, or from obligations framed in related terms such as transparency and non-discrimination.

detail.abstract: This article presents a selective critical review of AI governance scholarship circulated through the SSRN Legal Scholarship Network during September 2026. From a corpus of more than one hundred research entries identified in the monitored SSRN alerts, the author selects a limited number of works considered particularly significant for their legal arguments, competing doctrinal approaches, methodological implications, and potential contributions to the development of AI governance. The review is deliberately selective and does not purport to provide an exhaustive survey of SSRN publications or AI governance scholarship beyond the specified period. The analysis examines competing approaches to legal attribution, artificial intelligence accountability, human oversight, professional responsibility, and institutional governance. Particular attention is given to the originality and coherence of legal arguments, the reliability of cited authorities, the adequacy of supporting evidence, and the distinction between technological capabilities and legally attributable responsibility. The article evaluates both the contributions and limitations of the selected works, identifying areas of doctrinal convergence, unresolved disagreements, methodological weaknesses, and emerging research directions. Its purpose is not to establish a hierarchy of scholarly publications but to advance a substantive, evidence-based academic discussion grounded in critical examination of original texts and verifiable sources.

title: Global Flood Risk in the 2026/27 El Niño: An Empirical Estimate from the Historical Relationship
affiliations: World Bank

detail.title: Global Flood Risk in the 2026/27 El Niño: An Empirical Estimate from the Historical Relationship
detail.abstract: We estimate the response of recorded flood activity to the Niño3.4 sea-surface-temperature anomaly for 104 countries, using a monthly country panel built from EM-DAT (1980–2025) and the NOAA Niño3.4 series. Identification comes from within-country, within-calendar-month variation in the index, net of a linear trend in reporting intensity. The headline outcome is the expected number of recorded floods, estimated by quasi-Poisson regression; a logistic model of flood occurrence is reported alongside and gives near-identical answers. El Niño redistributes flood activity but does not change significantly the world total. The analysis finds an increase in the number of floods in 44 countries, with this increase significant in 10 countries. Country effects are large and geographically coherent, from 2.26 per °C in Uruguay to 0.46 in Togo. Applying the ECMWF Niño3.4 outlook against a neutral counterfactual, the expected number of recorded floods in these countries rises by 2.05× in 2026 and 2.88× in 2027. In parallel, the analysis suggests a decrease in the number of floods in 60 countries, with this decrease significant in 19 countries. In absolute terms, the countries with a positive signal are expected to record +42.9 additional floods in 2026 and +57.1 in 2027 on the main scenario, while the countries with a negative signal are expected to record 31.0 fewer floods in 2026 and 30.6 fewer in 2027. The two largely offset, leaving net changes of +11.8 and +26.5 events. As a comparison, the estimates agree in sign with the model-based El Niño flood signal of Ward et al. (2014) for 86% of the 29 countries whose estimated effect is significant. A reduced expected flood count does not imply reduced risk. The estimates describe a shift in the expected rate at which countries enter the disaster register; they place no bound on the severity of individual events. Damaging floods are recorded in every ENSO phase, and in countries with high floodplain exposure a single event within a suppressed season can exceed the annual average loss by a large margin. The results do not support any reduction in preparedness.

detail.abstract: Small businesses increasingly use Facebook and Instagram as low-cost channels for customer communication, promotion and market reach, yet evidence from Bangladesh remains limited regarding the mechanisms through which platform usefulness is translated into digital marketing capability and sustained platform use. This study develops and empirically examines an integrated Technology Acceptance Model (TAM)-Resource-Based View (RBV) framework in which perceived business usefulness is positioned as a technology-level antecedent, digital marketing capability as a capability mechanism, satisfaction/confirmation as a post-use evaluative mechanism, and continued use intention as the downstream behavioural outcome. The analysis uses 385 complete responses from the supplied Group-3 Meta database. Data screening included missingness checks, attention-check verification, duplicate-pattern inspection and straight-line response diagnostics. Reflective measurement was assessed through indicator loadings, composite reliability, average variance extracted and heterotrait-monotrait ratios. A PLS-SEM-compatible composite-score procedure with 5,000 bootstrap resamples was used to estimate structural paths and indirect effects. Perceived business usefulness positively predicts digital marketing capability (β=0.283, p<0.001), while both perceived usefulness (β=0.192) and capability (β=0.340) predict satisfaction. Continued-use intention is explained by perceived usefulness (β=0.211), digital marketing capability (β=0.243) and satisfaction (β=0.247), with all paths significant at p<0.001. The results indicate that perceived platform value is not merely an adoption belief; it is associated with a capability-building sequence that culminates in stronger continuation intentions. The study contributes a capability-oriented interpretation of TAM for social-commerce contexts and provides evidence from an emerging-market setting while maintaining a clear distinction between perceived user outcomes and objective SME performance.

detail.abstract: The value chain smile is a popular concept stating that upstream and downstream activities create more value than midstream activities and, therefore, firms should move toward an end of the value chain. Prior studies test this proposition using upstreamness measures anchored to final demand and find inconsistent evidence about the existence and morphology of the smile. We develop a local value chain curve anchored on a focal firm that maps its margin relative to those of its direct and indirect suppliers and customers. We find that firms with higher R&D and SG&A intensities are more likely to occupy the top of their local value chains. Transitions into the inverted-U shape are associated with persistently high R&D intensity and increased SG&A intensity, without systematic changes in the firm's upstreamness position. These findings help reconcile previous mixed evidence on the value-chain smile and identify firm capabilities associated with superior relative margin capture in local supply networks.

title: The Spotter Rule: Who Does the Work When AI Enters the Classroom
affiliations: University of Maryland Global Campus

detail.title: The Spotter Rule: Who Does the Work When AI Enters the Classroom

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Conflicts of Interest. The author declares no conflicts of interest. He has no affiliation with The New Yorker, with Dan Rockmore, or with any AI company. Positionality. The author is a tenured professor who teaches cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, cloud technologies, and project management at the University of Maryland Global Campus, and a Fulbright Specialist. He has more than three decades of experience across academia, Silicon Valley engineering, and entrepreneurship on three continents. He played college soccer, has coached youth soccer for twenty-five years, has run marathons, and has trained with a paid personal trainer for the past ten years. These experiences shape his view of the difference between helping a learner and doing the work for them. He teaches many students online, which informs Section 6. Generative AI Use. The author used Claude (Anthropic) to help locate and summarize sources, organize the argument, and edit for plain-language clarity. All arguments, the Spotter Rule itself, and the conclusions are the author's own. The author reviewed every factual claim against its source and is fully responsible for the content. Data Availability. No new data were generated. All sources are listed in the References.

detail.abstract: In a September 2026 essay in The New Yorker, Dartmouth professor Dan Rockmore asked whether the classroom should be more like the gym, a place where the effort is the point. The metaphor is strong, but it leaves a practical question open: who may use artificial intelligence for what? This viewpoint answers with one sentence, the Spotter Rule: AI may spot, but it may not lift. A spotter sets up the bar, keeps the lifter safe, calls out form, and adjusts the load. A spotter never lifts the weight and never signs the lifter's log. The distinction between assistance and substitution is not new. This paper's contribution is to make it usable in three ways. First, each course must name its own "rep," the specific thinking the course exists to build, so that AI use is judged against the learning objective rather than against whether AI was used at all. Second, the same rule must bind professors as well as students, which removes a double standard found in many campus policies. Third, assessments should be designed so the rep is visible. The paper also argues that AI does not send anyone to the gym: tools can remind and encourage, but the decision to participate remains the learner's. It grounds the rule in learning science and in recent experimental evidence, applies it to three course settings, addresses accessibility and disability accommodations, and offers a three-step decision test for faculty, presented as a flowchart. It is an analytical position for discussion, not a tested intervention.

detail.abstract: Political incentives to raise school quality are often weak in decentralized education systems. In this context, officeholders with professional knowledge of education and strong attachment to the sector may shape public-service delivery. This paper examines the effects of electing mayors with education-sector backgrounds (hereafter, educators) on student learning and teacher wages in Brazilian municipal elections from 2004 to 2016. I use a politician-characteristic regression discontinuity design that compares municipalities where educator candidates barely win with those where they barely lose. Test-score improvements under educator mayors' terms are modest and increasing, rising from 0.005 to 0.068 standard deviations, but are imprecisely estimated. Notably, the largest learning gains occur five years after the election, after the next municipal election, when test scores rise by 0.16 standard deviations. I find no evidence that educator mayors generate broad wage gains for teachers. Consistent with this finding, there is also no detectable effect on total municipal spending on education. Instead, the evidence better aligns with changes in school personnel, particularly greater stability and experience of school principals. Overall, the findings suggest that politicians' professional backgrounds in education can influence local public service delivery through changes in school leadership.

title: Loyal To A Fault? The Threat Of Llms Producing Biased Responses Favoring Their Own Self-Interest

detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to exhibit numerous biases inherited from the human-generated data on which they are trained. This Essay examines a distinct and previously unmeasured category, that of self-interest bias. This is the potential tendency of an LLM to provide responses that favor the commercial, reputational, or legal interests of the model or its parent company. Given the billions of dollars invested in these models, the litigation and regulatory exposure their parent companies face, and the documented tendency of AI systems to behave in self-protective ways, the threat of self-interest bias is pronounced. This Essay situates this issue within the literature on external LLM bias, the push for AI regulation, potential legal liability, the commercial incentives driving LLM development, and the growing use of LLMs by judges and attorneys.

detail.abstract: IFRS S2 and Hong Kong's new climate requirements ask firms to disclose the current and anticipated financial effects of climate risk, informed by scenario analysis. Until now, research on these disclosures has been largely qualitative: content analysis, disclosure indices and counts of whether a topic is present. The numbers themselves are scattered across hundreds of report pages, tables, charts and footnotes. We use a large language model with page-cited, schemaconstrained extraction to turn them into data for 140 Hong Kong large caps over FY2024-FY2025 (267 reports, 42,192 pages). Each label is checked against the source pages under written rules. The gap is wide. Under a deliberately broad definition, which counts any climateattributed number including bounds, ranges and pilot subsets, quantified disclosure rises from 13.8% of reports in FY2024 to 34.3% in FY2025. Under a strict definition, which requires scenario-and horizon-tied effects for both physical and transition risk, it rises from 1.5% to 6.6%. Most quantified effects are bounds, ranges and ratios. Only 9 of 267 report-years contain a scenario-tied absolute amount. Markets do not visibly price the difference. Equity returns, volume, volatility and distance-to-default around report releases do not differ by disclosure level; the minimum detectable three-day abnormal return is about 1.6%. Interbank MTN spreads for the A+H and onshore-subsidiary subsample (54-62 bonds, 8-10 issuers) are uninformative, and the disclosure effect cannot be separated from the FY2025 regulatory step. Disclosure without comparable numbers is not priced at any economically moderate magnitude.

detail.abstract: Whether generative AI raises or lowers the demand for labour depends on the new work it creates. I measure that new work directly in 18.6 million duty statements from US job postings, 2019-2026, drawn from a new dataset built from applicant-tracking-system pages archived by Common Crawl. A duty is new when nothing in early-2019 postings is close to it. In the third of occupations that use AI most, genuinely new work rose from about one in every 100 duty lines in 2022 to nearly five in 2026, four-fifths of it work on AI itself. Its mix is shifting from building AI systems to working with them: using AI tools and driving their adoption. Genuinely new tasks that are not about AI remain rare, and half of the new AI duties have no related task in their occupation's O*NET list. The pay premium for AI duties is mostly sorting.

detail.abstract: How do liquidity shocks affect drug sales? Building on prior work on search costs in pharmaceutical markets, we propose that liquidity constraints have a larger impact on the drug sales of less recurring acute ailments than chronic ailments which have steady consumption. We exploit demonetization in India in 2016 as a transitory negative liquidity shock. Units, value, and weight of acute drug sales experienced a relatively higher decline than those for chronic illnesses. Consistent with the search cost hypothesis, we find that the impact varies by close correlates of search, such as drug price dispersion, government-mandated stock-keeping and availability of public health infrastructure. Our work contributes by showing how the constrained liquidity of households can have differential effects on the downstream market structure of retail drugs.

detail.abstract:
Background: Recently, a phase II study (the Evolution trial) investigated a radiotherapy-free chemoimmunotherapy strategy in patients with unresectable locally advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and PD-L1 tumor proportion score (TPS) ≥50%, demonstrating durable disease control. Direct comparative evidence between radiotherapy-free strategy and chemoradiotherapy, whether delivered concurrently (cCRT) or sequentially (sCRT), remains lacking. Therefore, this study aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety among different therapeutic strategies in patients with PD-L1 TPS ≥50% unresectable stage III NSCLC using a real-world matching-adjusted indirect comparison (MAIC), and to further investigate the critical role of thoracic radiotherapy in the immunotherapy era.

Methods: An unanchored MAIC was performed to compare clinical outcomes between cCRT/sCRT followed by immunotherapy consolidation and radiotherapy-free chemoimmunotherapy strategy in patients with unresectable stage III NSCLC and PD-L1 TPS ≥50%. Data for the radiotherapy-free group were derived from the Evolution trial. Individual patient data (IPD) for the cCRT/sCRT cohort were obtained from a multicenter real-world cohort of patients treated at three Chinese cancer centers between January 1, 2019, and July 31, 2025, with eligibility criteria aligned with those of the Evolution trial. The primary endpoint was overall survival (OS). Secondary endpoints included progression-free survival (PFS), objective response rate (ORR), complete response (CR), and treatment-related adverse events (AEs).

Findings: After MAIC adjustment, patients receiving cCRT/sCRT followed by immunotherapy consolidation demonstrated significantly improved OS compared with those receiving radiotherapy-free chemoimmunotherapy (hazard ratio [HR] = 0.26, 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.10-0.67; P = 0.005). PFS showed a favorable trend in the cCRT/sCRT group. The two strategies showed distinct toxicity profiles. Although the cCRT/sCRT group experienced a higher incidence of all-grade pneumonitis (odds ratio [OR] = 6.73; 95% CI, 1.74-26.0), the incidence of grade ≥3 pneumonitis was similar between groups (OR = 1.04, 95% CI, 0.18-5.96). Conversely, patients receiving radiotherapy-free chemoimmunotherapy had a higher incidence of grade ≥3 treatment-related AEs (OR = 0.12, 95% CI, 0.04-0.40). Sensitivity analyses restricted to patients receiving cCRT showed significantly improved OS (HR = 0.10, 95% CI, 0.02-0.54, P = 0.007) and PFS (HR = 0.19, 95% CI, 0.05-0.68, P = 0.011) compared with radiotherapy-free chemoimmunotherapy.

Interpretation: Among patients with PD-L1 TPS ≥50% unresectable stage III NSCLC, cCRT/sCRT combined with immunotherapy consolidation was associated with  improved OS compared with radiotherapy-free chemoimmunotherapy. All-grade pneumonitis was more frequent with cCRT/sCRT, whereas overall grade ≥3 treatment-related AEs were less frequent than with radiotherapy-free chemoimmunotherapy. In the immunotherapy era, thoracic radiotherapy may remain an important component of curative-intent treatment for unresectable NSCLC with high PD-L1 expression. Longer-term follow-up and prospective studies are warranted to confirm these findings.

detail.abstract:
​Background: Acute exacerbations of generalized myasthenia gravis (gMG) require rapidprompt rescue treatment, butbut comparative evidence regardingon the clinical effectiveness and economic burden of plasma exchange (PE), intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), and efgartigimod (EFG) remains limited. 

Methods: We conducted a retrospective multicenter study using clinical and economic data from 15 hospitals in China. Patients hospitalized for acute exacerbation of gMG between April 1, 2019, and April 1, 2025, were screened. Admissions involving PE, IVIG, or EFG alone were included in the primary three-group analysis, while sequential treatment regimens were evaluated separately in an exploratory sensitivity analysis. Treatment-group balance was addressed using multinomial propensity scores and generalized overlap weighting. The primary efficacy and economic outcomes were QMG improvement and total hospital cost, respectively, with Holm adjustment for multiple comparisons.

Findings: Of 475 admissions screened, 374 admissions among 333 unique patients met the eligibility criteria, including 169 PE, 83 IVIG, 67 EFG, and 55 sequential-treatment admissions. The primary three-group analysis included 319 admissions. After overlap weighting, QMG improvement was greater with IVIG than with PE (adjusted mean difference 2.760 points, 95% CI 1.077–4.443; Holm-adjusted P=0.007), with EFG than with PE (5.197, 3.703–6.692; P<0.001), and with EFG than with IVIG (2.438, 0.621–4.254; P=0.019). Total hospital cost was higher with IVIG than with PE (ratio of adjusted means 1.599, 95% CI 1.193–2.143; Holm-adjusted P=0.007) and lower with EFG than with IVIG (0.595, 0.446–0.794; P=0.003), whereas EFG and PE did not differ significantly. As secondary findings, rescue-treatment costs and MG-related drug costs were higher with both IVIG and EFG than with PE, while the MG-ADL findings were sensitive to missing-data assumptions. However, after exclusion of the largest contributing center, none of the QMG or total-cost comparisons remained statistically significant. In subgroup analysis, no QMG or MG-ADL subgroup interaction was supported after Benjamini–Hochberg correction. Interactions were identified only for rescue-treatment cost by MGFA severity and pre-intervention clinical state.

Conclusions: EFG was associated with greater short-term QMG improvement than PE, without evidence of higher total hospital costs. These findings support EFG as a potential rescue-treatment option, although the sensitivity of the estimates to center composition warrants prospective confirmation.

detail.abstract: This paper traces a single line-the evolution of the sign: from the honest, costly signal that sexual selection made of the display trait, through mimicry, standardization, and perception, to human symbols: knightly heraldry, state coats of arms, corporate logos, and signs of jurisdictions. The market is read as a late chapter in this evolution. The display trait is defined as a sign on the basis of which the evaluating party renders a verdict before combat and before comparing products. The paper shows how concepts from the biology of signaling-sexual selection, the handicap principle, the true referent and the center of gravity of value, Batesian, Müllerian, and aggressive mimicry, ritualization, the supernormal stimulus, the search image, and the laws of perception-and cognitive mechanisms of status-the mere-exposure effect, processing fluency, prototypicality, the recognition heuristic, conditioned reflex, orienting reflex, psychological distance, the law of generalization, and affect-are transferred to the market and generate testable hypotheses concerning display selection among signs, frequency dependence of counterfeiting, a shared honest sign, the status loop, and the hierarchy of signs. The central section answers how a logo acquires status and hierarchy: at the cognitive level, through the loop "exposure → fluency → trust → choice"; at the social level, through prestige, positional goods, and distinction. The hierarchy of signs mirrors a trophic pyramid: there are few apex signs, and they capture a disproportionate share of capacity. The line culminates in the sign of a jurisdiction: state symbols as a country's display trait, entering the formula for its capacity twice. The trophic structure of the market-the chain of production stages, Lindeman's rule, pyramids, carrying capacity, predator-prey dynamics, cascades, decomposition, invasions-is retained as the environment in which signs live: the sign does not create resources; it distributes them. The paper situates itself among seven neighboring fieldsfrom evolutionary economics to semiotics and the brand-equity literature-and is described as a research programme in Lakatos's sense: the register comprises forty-nine entries-forty-eight hypotheses at different stages of operationalization (including candidate hypotheses 45 and 47) and one clarification (49)-and each entry's status is explicitly distinguished. Each transfer is formulated as a separately numbered hypothesis with its own empirical test; the limits of the analogy-eight breaks-are listed in a separate section. The methodological principle is that analogy is a tool for generating hypotheses, not proof.

detail.abstract: Risk parity (RP) is a popular form of risk budgeting that is used in the modern portfolio theory. The RP portfolios (RPPs) can be used as an alternative to the classical mean variance portfolio (MVP) framework since the latter suffers from high sensitivity to its input parameters (asset price volatility and, particularly, expected returns). In this work, we expand the RP formalism by replacing Pearson’s correlations with partial correlations (PC). If the latter are conditioned on total market return, they increase multi-sector equity portfolio diversity and may lead to a higher portfolio performance and more stable weights out-of-sample. Here we compare performance of the PC-based RPP (PartRPP) consisting of 12 major equity sector ETFs with the Pearson’s-based RPP (PearRPP), equal-weight portfolio (EWP), minimum variance MVPs (PearMinVP and PartMinVP) and maximum Sharpe MVPs (PearMVP and PartMVP) in 2007 - 2025. Somewhat paradoxically, PCs increase the Technology ETF (XLK) weight and, hence, decrease RPP diversity. This XLK “de-risking” effect happens because XLK may have only negative PCs with all other sector ETFs. As a result, PartRPP, PartMinVP and PartMVP outperform PearRPP, PearMinVP and PearMVP, respectively. For our ETF-based portfolio, MVP on average outperforms the other models considered in this work. We also checked the portfolio performance sensitivity to the calibration window lengths used for estimation of expected returns and volatility.

detail.abstract: Smart Money Concepts (SMC) is one of the most widely marketed retail trading methods, yet its claims have not been tested in the peer-reviewed literature. We implement a production SMC indicator as a fully rule-based intraday strategy on spot gold, using one-minute data from 2012 to 2026, and pre-register every test. To isolate entry timing, each signal is paired with random entries that share its side, stop, and target. Timing contributes nothing: under every regime filter, target rule and benchmark the timing component is indistinguishable from zero, and at a one-hour horizon a positive effect as small as 0.01R per trade is rejected. Returns that exist come from a slow trend filter and the exit rule. Net of spread and financing, they are positive only in the 2021-2026 bull market and never statistically significant. Two independent price feeds produce almost entirely different signals but the same aggregate returns. We also show that the common symmetric random-entry benchmark is biased upward for trend-gated strategies by 0.06-0.23R per trade here, and makes a neutral rule look harmful. Across ten markets, cost relative to the structural stop decides outcomes, and no market is profitable in every period. A trend filter alone is not a viable strategy once financing is charged.

detail.abstract: Is unequal access to health care unjust and, if so, under what circumstances? This article attempts to answer these questions by inquiring to what extent inequality in access to medical care conflicts with the idea that everyone's life is of equal moral worth. This inquiry yields three conclusions: First, everyone must have sufficient access to medical care, due to the linkages between health care and health and the ways in which access to health care bears on respect for people. Second, certain kinds of inequality in access to medical care serve to demean people and create or reinforce social hierarchies. Third, although sufficient access does not always require equal access, what counts as "sufficient" access to health care is comparative and, more specifically, it entails that everyone should have at least roughly the same level of access to health care as most members of their society. In addition, this article offers a novel account of why health care is special, or morally distinctive. It proposes that wrongful discrimination in access to health care and the failure to provide health care are especially damaging to people's self-respect because of health care's distinctive organizing purpose: maintaining or restoring human health.

detail.abstract:
The Indic Futures Paper Series has, across six papers and one companion governance paper, documented the systematic engineering of individual human cognition and developed a complete counter-architecture for the sovereign mind at the individual, institutional, educational, and political-economy levels. A structural gap has remained unaddressed: the series has established what cognitive capture does to the individual mind and what sovereign minds require in order to be formed. It has not directly addressed what manufactured belonging, algorithmic information homogenisation, and tribal identity activation do to the collective mind — to the group’s capacity for genuine deliberation, honest exchange, and the emergence of collective intelligence that exceeds what any individual member could produce alone. This paper addresses that gap.

The paper introduces the Collective Capture Mechanism (CCM) as the series’ account of how the Want Architecture’s operations, applied to groups rather than individuals, systematically destroy the conditions that generate genuine collective intelligence. The CCM operates through six pathways: Information Homogenisation (the algorithmic convergence of group members’ information environments toward a shared tribal feed), Dissent Suppression (the social punishment of perspectives that challenge the group’s manufactured consensus), Tribal Veto (the blocking of valid information on the grounds of its source’s tribal identity), Synthetic Consensus (the mistaking of manufactured agreement for genuine deliberative convergence), Epistemic Echo (the progressive narrowing of the group’s evaluative frame through positive feedback loops), and Authority Capture (the colonisation of the group’s epistemic process by the preferences of its most dominant member).

Against the CCM, the paper introduces the Sovereign Collective Intelligence Framework (SCIF) — five conditions derived from the Indic tradition’s three foundational concepts of collective knowing: Sabha (the deliberative assembly and its structural requirements for genuine collective intelligence), Sangha (the community of practitioners and its relational requirements for epistemic trust and honest exchange), and Samvad (the conversational practice of genuine dialogue, as distinct from debate, performance, and manufactured consensus). The SCIF’s five conditions are: Sabha Standard (structural conditions for genuine deliberation), Sangha Coefficient (relational quality of the deliberating community), Samvad Protocol (conversational architecture for collective knowing), Collective Viveka Quotient (CVQ — a group-level measure of discriminative capacity), and Collective Sakshi (the group’s capacity for collective witnessing of its own epistemic processes).

Five application domains are developed: democratic legislatures and gram sabhas, organisational boards and leadership teams, AI-mediated public deliberation, community conflict resolution, and scientific and research communities. Two testable propositions are stated. The paper positions the SCIF as the series’ collective-level counter-architecture, completing the framework’s coverage from the individual (Papers No. 0–5) through the institutional (Papers No. 4, 6) to the collective: the level at which democratic, organisational, and community intelligence is either cultivated or systematically destroyed.


Not peer-reviewed. Circulated for scholarly discussion. APA 7. AI Disclosure: AI-based tools assisted with literature search and language editing. All analysis, framework design, and conclusions are the author's own.

detail.abstract: An earnings release can provide information about what managers will discuss on the forthcoming conference call, but investors may already anticipate that information. We examine what the release adds using prediction markets where contracts pay when specified words are spoken during the call. Their prices reflect expectations about those words, allowing us to observe how expectations change when the release becomes public. Release wording helps predict call content beyond patterns in earlier releases and calls, and words appearing in the release are associated with upward price revisions. However, predictions based on contract prices before the release do not clearly improve when we add the release's wording. These findings connect firms' current disclosures to expectations about their forthcoming communication.

title: Will Fixed Book Prices Fix It? Common Agency and Vertical Integration of Publishers and Bookstores
affiliations: NHH Norwegian School of Economics, University of Minho and NHH Norwegian School of Economics, NHH Norwegian School of Economics

detail.title: Will Fixed Book Prices Fix It? Common Agency and Vertical Integration of Publishers and Bookstores
detail.abstract: Book markets are characterised by common distribution through competing bookstores and vertical integration between publishers and bookstore chains, and in many countries publishers are allowed to set fixed book prices (FBP) in the bookstores. Under vertical separation, FBP can reduce retail prices when publishers have sufficiently strong bargaining power, as the elimination of double marginalisation outweighs the loss of intra-brand competition. We show that vertical integration fundamentally changes this trade-off. It eliminates double marginalisation inside the chain, thereby substantially reducing the scope for FBP to lower retail prices. But since FBP eliminates retail price differences on the same title, the allocative distortions are reduced when imposing FBP and consumer welfare and total welfare are no longer aligned. We find that, in the presence of vertical integration, the introduction of FBP is less likely to benefit consumers and more likely to benefit publishers than in an industry with vertical separation.

detail.title: Who Can Produce What? Firm Capabilities and Product Entry
detail.abstract: Which firms supply which products? Modeling multi-product firms under heterogeneous markups, we recover firms' costs for produced products and develop an algorithm inspired by recommender systems to predict costs for unproduced products. Lower predicted costs imply increased product adoption and identify which firms enter when export demand rises, including firms crossing broad product classifications. We use these counterfactual costs to quantify how reductions in fixed and marginal costs induce product entry and lower price indices. In a price-stabilization exercise following a cost shock, entry subsidies can cost less than subsidies to incumbents, particularly for smaller shocks when capable potential entrants remain available.
